title: The Life of One Saved Order
note: Prototype storyboard contract. Each scene is a projection of research.json claims: `claims` holds 0-based indexes into research.json concepts['oracle-architecture'].claims. Nothing may appear in a scene that is not in the research artifact.

scenes.title: Two things with one name
scenes.caption: People say "the database" and mean one thing. It is two. The files on disk keep the orders when the lights are off. The memory and the little worker crew — the "instance" — are awake only while it runs. The whole story is these two halves talking.

scenes.title: The ask arrives
scenes.caption: The order app says: save this order. A server process picks it up and first checks the shared pool: have we heard this exact kind of ask before? If yes, reuse the old plan (a soft parse). If no, build a new one — that costs more.

scenes.title: Fetch the shelf, not the warehouse
scenes.caption: The block that holds this customer's rows is copied from the datafile into the buffer cache — the working table in memory. Changes never happen down on the disk shelf. They happen on the copy.

scenes.title: The change happens in memory
scenes.caption: The row is changed on the cached copy, which is now "dirty" — different from its disk twin. Two notes are written at the same moment: a redo note (how to redo this change) and an undo note (how to take it back). The datafile has not been touched.

scenes.title: COMMIT — the only write that matters now
scenes.caption: The app says COMMIT. LGWR takes the redo notes and writes them to the online redo log on disk. The session waits for exactly that one write ("log file sync") — then "done" goes back to the app. The order's data block is still only in memory. That is fine: the redo note on disk is the promise.

scenes.title: The slow tidy-up
scenes.caption: Later, on its own schedule, DBWn copies dirty blocks down to the datafiles. CKPT moves a bookmark — the checkpoint — forward in the control file and datafile headers: everything before this point is safely on disk. No one is waiting on any of this.

scenes.title: The power goes out. The order survives.
scenes.caption: Crash. Memory is gone — the dirty block with it. On restart, SMON replays the redo log from the checkpoint forward, rebuilding every promised change; then undo rolls back whatever was never committed. The committed order comes back. That is why COMMIT waited on the redo write and nothing else.
